distilled_summary: When sharing integration examples through the Rock KB, cite public repositories or official documentation and keep instance-specific endpoints, credentials, and operational context out of the public contribution row.
title: Use public source links for integration examples

distilled_summary: When a Lava entity command uses `where:`, Rock parses the rendered string as a Dynamic LINQ expression. In deploy scripts, composing that expression from captured rows, loop variables, or values that may render blank can make the whole entity command fail before any row is returned. Prefer literal values for simple lookups; for rerunnable configuration deploys, resolve existing row IDs with read-only SQL by stable natural keys, then use `modify{Entity}` for the actual write. If an entity-command `where:` fails unexpectedly, inspect the fully rendered expression and check for blank IDs, unescaped quotes, mixed operators, or values that belong in a parameterized SQL lookup instead.
title: Treat entity-command where clauses as a brittle Dynamic LINQ boundary

distilled_summary: For workflow configuration deploys written in Lava, make each step idempotent. First resolve the parent object by a stable key, modify it, then re-query the canonical ID before writing children. Apply this to workflow types, workflow attributes, activity types, action types, forms, form attributes, and action setting values. Do not carry a blank ID, a desired GUID from a create path, or an unverified `ModifyResult` object into dependent writes. For workflow attributes, explicitly scope every attribute to the actual workflow type with `EntityTypeId` for Workflow, `EntityTypeQualifierColumn = WorkflowTypeId`, and the actual workflow type ID as `EntityTypeQualifierValue`. Print the resolved IDs and verify the final shape before wiring the workflow to a live trigger.
title: Use a two-phase pattern for rerunnable workflow ModifyEntity deploys

distilled_summary: Workflow action component settings are stored as `AttributeValue` rows. The setting `AttributeId` belongs to the action component's setting attribute, and `EntityId` is the `WorkflowActionType.Id` being configured. For deploy scripts, resolve the action type ID after the action exists, then write explicit setting rows with verified setting attribute IDs. Avoid broad deletes and avoid parsing setting IDs out of free-form captured text. If a setting is a workflow attribute reference, store the workflow attribute GUID expected by that action component. Because component setting attribute IDs can vary by Rock version and plugin set, verify them in the target instance before reuse.
title: Workflow action settings are AttributeValue rows attached to the action type

distilled_summary: Before changing or troubleshooting a Rock REST API integration, identify the exact controller route, the authenticated identity or REST key, the security grants that identity depends on, and whether the request should be read-only or write-capable. Validate the API behavior against public documentation and the target Rock version before broadening permissions. Treat a successful test call as only one signal: agents should still confirm least-privilege scope, logging, token handling, and rollback expectations before recommending production use.
title: Preflight REST API work by checking identity, endpoint, and permission scope

distilled_summary: For Helix pages that use HTMX active-search or live filters, distinguish a page-hosted Lava Application Content block from a bare call to the underlying `/api/v2/lava-app/...` endpoint. Build the first paint so the page renders useful content server-side, then let HTMX requests use the caret route form from inside the content block. Before using the same endpoint on a public or anonymous page, test it as an anonymous visitor and as the intended authenticated role; if the endpoint depends on block/runtime authentication or the data set is small enough to ship once, prefer a server-rendered list with client-side filtering and a no-JavaScript fallback. Do not treat a working staff-session HTMX request as proof that the endpoint is a safe public API.
title: Run Helix active-search through the Lava Application Content block boundary

distilled_summary: When troubleshooting room availability or planned capacity for Rock check-in, inspect two different relationships. Room capacity thresholds live on the `Location` record, so a `SoftRoomThreshold` change applies to that room wherever it is reused; it is not scoped to one service time or schedule. Schedule availability is a separate group-location relationship: verify that the check-in group has the expected `GroupLocation`, that the `GroupLocation` points to the intended room, and that the correct schedule is linked through `GroupLocationSchedule` or the schedule collection exposed for that group location. A useful preflight report joins group, group location, location, and schedule, then compares room name, threshold, and schedule link before changing production configuration.
title: Verify check-in room capacity separately from schedule availability

distilled_summary: Before trusting an event-registration dashboard, name each metric grain and population explicitly. Count RegistrationRegistrant rows for people and distinct Registration rows for registration records; do not label them interchangeably. Define confirmed and wait-list predicates once, apply them to every chart, and test invariants such as confirmed people equaling the sum of mutually exclusive segments and each one-value distribution. Test a multi-person registration, a wait-list registrant, and a recent registrant. For historical pace, align events by days remaining until registration closes rather than calendar date. Do not require many-to-many department totals to equal unique people; disclose that exception and validate it separately.
title: Reconcile event registration dashboard metrics by grain and population

distilled_summary: When a registration report segments people by staff, serving, or department, document the local truth source instead of presenting the categories as built-in universal Rock semantics. Use only active, non-archived memberships in reviewed groups, apply an explicit mutually exclusive precedence such as staff before serving, and reconcile the segment total to confirmed registrants. Gate department reporting behind a reviewed serving verifier when that is the operating definition, preserve a verifier-only or unassigned bucket, and disclose that one person may count in multiple departments. Leave the module disabled when the target instance cannot define and validate the groups or hierarchy.
title: Treat staff and serving segments as configured local truth with explicit precedence

distilled_summary: After an exact Rock file-content readback confirms the intended Helix or Lava Application source was saved, validate the rendered dashboard as a separate gate. Test an unauthorized visitor, the intended staff role, and an administrator without treating admin override as proof of role access. Assert known metric invariants and representative rows, inspect visible and hidden Lava error surfaces plus browser-console errors, exercise filters and empty states, and measure responsive layout for clipped labels, unintended internal vertical scrolling, and bounded horizontal overflow. Content equality proves deployment targeting; rendered checks prove authorization, data semantics, JavaScript behavior, and layout in the actual page context.
title: Validate rendered Helix dashboards after exact content readback

distilled_summary: When building a Rock API v2 integration that owns only a few fields on an entity, prefer PATCH over PUT. Treat PUT as a full-object update path that requires the caller to understand every relevant model property and default; omitted values can become destructive depending on the endpoint and model shape. Before writing, inspect the API v2 docs and Model Map, grant the narrowest read/write controller permission to the integration role or REST key, test against a non-production record, then read the entity back and compare only the fields the integration intended to own.
title: Prefer API v2 PATCH for integration-owned partial updates

distilled_summary: Before exposing an Entity Search through API v2 or Lava entity commands, verify the search entity type matches the endpoint entity, the search has a stable key, Execute permission is granted intentionally, and query size is bounded with take and maximum-result settings. Test Include Paths rather than assuming eager loading is always helpful; it can fix missing related data but can also hurt performance or security behavior. For public or semi-public consumers, validate the rendered Dynamic LINQ, apply the narrowest permission scope, and run a readback query that proves the returned shape is limited to the expected fields.
title: Preflight Entity Search before using it through API v2 or Lava

distilled_summary: For public seasonal features such as group finders, registration lists, or mobile-facing CMS content, closing the season should verify more than a Lava date flag or template setting. Check the public page route, any redirects, block-level authorization, mobile or alternate surfaces, and the underlying filters that decide what can still be shown or submitted. When inspecting Rock security rows, include the secured entity type as part of the lookup so a Page ID is not confused with a Block ID that happens to share the same integer value.
title: Close public seasonal features by checking block security and routes, not only Lava flags

distilled_summary: For signed-document workflows, reports, and reminder DataViews, base completion checks on `SignatureDocument` joined through the applies-to person alias and scoped to the intended `SignatureDocumentTemplate`. A person attribute such as a signed date can be useful for display, but it can drift from the actual document record and should not be the only source used for suppression or completion logic. Verify template scope, signed timestamp, and person alias linkage before excluding someone from future sends.
title: Use SignatureDocument rows as the source of truth for signed-document completion

distilled_summary: When a workflow sends a short-lived verification code, separate the operational code needed for delivery from the long-term audit state needed for verification. Store a hash, expiration, attempt count, and verified flag for server-side checking, and consider disabling or limiting communication history for the plain code message if the code should not remain visible after use. Verify the communication medium, sender, recipient person attribute, and retention behavior before enabling the flow broadly.
title: Avoid retaining plain SMS verification codes in communication history when not needed

distilled_summary: A signed-document workflow can often serve both connection-request launches and bulk audience launches, but connection-state actions must be guarded. Keep the signature, communication, and document steps independent of connection updates, and run connection-status or connection-request mutations only when the workflow actually has a ConnectionRequest context. This lets connection-driven launches continue normal pipeline behavior without letting mass-send launches accidentally change connection records.
title: Guard connection-mutating actions when one signed-document workflow supports both pipeline and mass-send launches

distilled_summary: When a workflow charges a previously saved payment account, do not trust a selected saved-account ID by itself. Revalidate that the saved account belongs to the expected payer, belongs to the intended gateway, uses an eligible reusable payment type, and still exists immediately before charging. The authorization form may present a friendly label, but the payment action should operate on verified saved-account identity and should fail closed when the account is missing, revoked, wallet-only, or tied to a different payer or gateway.
title: Validate saved payment account ownership, gateway, and type before workflow-triggered charges

distilled_summary: A workflow Delay action is useful for scheduled follow-up charges or notices, but the world can change while the workflow is waiting. Before processing a delayed payment or other irreversible action, re-check the source workflow, authorization status, revocation state, saved-account eligibility, cancellation state, and any required audit metadata. Do not treat validation performed before the Delay as sufficient for the post-delay action, and make retries idempotent so a failed late step does not duplicate a charge or notification.
title: Revalidate authorization and cancellation state immediately before delayed workflow payments

distilled_summary: When a DataView or automation needs to know how long a ConnectionRequest has been in a specific status, calculate from status-change History rows rather than `ConnectionRequest.ModifiedDateTime`. ModifiedDateTime can be updated by notes, edits, assignments, or other changes unrelated to status movement. For age-based status automation, parse the ConnectionStatus history, select the latest transition into the source status, and compare that timestamp while also confirming the request is still in the expected current status.
title: Use History rows, not ModifiedDateTime, for ConnectionRequest status age

distilled_summary: When an Obsidian block action is the correct save path, do not treat a successful Save response as proof that the intended configuration persisted. First load the real admin page or block initialization, identify the block GUID, action key, and current server payload, then save through the block action and verify with an independent readback such as Edit, Preview, refreshed block initialization, a normal API read, or bounded read-only SQL. A BlockAction may return only a success signal while normalization, defaults, or ignored fields change the actual saved object.
title: Verify Obsidian BlockAction saves with an independent readback

distilled_summary: When deploying Rock-managed endpoint, block, or server-file content, a successful upload or file-content write is not enough. Capture the prior content or hash, deploy the intended content through the correct file-content surface, then read back the saved value or hash from Rock and compare it to the expected artifact. This is especially important for Lava endpoints and CMS/server-file edits where caches, route selection, or wrong file targets can make the live page differ from the local file that was uploaded.
title: Verify Rock file-content deployments with exact content readback

distilled_summary: When a communication list group is populated from a DataView, report, or SQL-backed targeting query, refresh the group membership immediately before sending and compare the group count to the source result count. Also test the call-to-action link with a representative valid person or alias parameter before launching the message. Communication lists are durable groups, so stale membership can survive after the underlying report changed; count alignment is the guardrail that the send audience still matches the intended targeting rule.
title: Refresh communication-list groups and compare them to the source count before sending

distilled_summary: For check-in room schedule changes, treat GroupLocationSchedule as a composite relationship between GroupLocation and Schedule, not as a normal entity with its own Id. A generated REST update to /api/GroupLocations/{id} updates scalar GroupLocation fields and should not be relied on to replace the Schedules navigation collection. When an Obsidian Check-in Schedule Builder block is available and authorized, its Save block action can be called with GroupLocation IdKeys and Schedule IdKeys to add or remove selected schedules through RockContext. Agents should first verify the target GroupLocation rows, Schedule records, block action availability, and permissions, then read back GroupLocationSchedule rows after the action completes.
title: Use the Obsidian Schedule Builder action for check-in GroupLocation schedule links

distilled_summary: When creating a GroupLocation through Rock's generated REST API, keep the payload to scalar GroupLocation fields unless the endpoint behavior has been tested on the target Rock version. Supplying partial navigation objects such as Schedules can create unintended related records instead of linking an existing record. If unintended placeholder schedules are created, first verify with read-only queries or API reads that they are accidental and not referenced by any other table or workflow path, then use the generated Schedule REST endpoint to delete only the proven accidental Schedule records. Always read back the GroupLocationSchedule relationships after cleanup.
title: Avoid partial navigation payloads when creating GroupLocations through REST

distilled_summary: When loading registration-driven check-in or camp groups through Rock's generated REST API, do not assume a successful POST to /api/GroupMembers returns a usable response body with the new Id. Treat the POST as the mutation, then read back the active GroupMember by the intended GroupId, PersonId, and GroupRoleId before patching RegistrationRegistrant.GroupMemberId. Make the loader idempotent by reusing exactly one matching active member row if it already exists and the registration is not linked. After the load, verify that every non-waitlist registrant links to an active GroupMember in the expected group and role, that waitlist registrants remain unlinked unless explicitly approved, and that duplicate GroupMemberId or PersonId placements do not exist.
title: Read back GroupMember creates before linking RegistrationRegistrant.GroupMemberId

distilled_summary: In the Check-In Label Designer, Custom Text with Dynamic Text enabled is different from Attendee Info, Check-in Info, and Achievement Info data-source text fields. Custom Dynamic Text renders the configured Lava template against merge fields created from the public properties of the label data object selected by the label type. For a Person label, useful top-level fields include Person, PersonAttendance, AllAttendance, Family, IsFirstTime, AreaNames, GroupNames, GroupRoleNames, LocationNames, ScheduleNames, SecurityCode, CheckInDateTime, CurrentDateTime, and achievement lists. Each PersonAttendance item is a label attendance detail with nested Person, Area, Group, Location, Schedule, Campus, Device, SearchType, Source, SecurityCode, StartDateTime, EndDateTime, and GroupMembers values. To read a checked-in group attribute on a Person label, assign the first PersonAttendance item and apply the Attribute filter to attendance.Group, for example Bus # from attendance.Group Attribute BusNumber. Data-source text fields should instead use the built-in Field dropdown because those values are supplied by FieldSourceHelper.GetDataSources for the current label type.
title: Use label data properties for Check-In Label Designer Dynamic Text

distilled_summary: When a Rock page ships a small result set and filters it client-side, make the rendered data attributes and the browser filter values use the same case and format. GUID comparisons should be normalized consistently. Short numeric IDs should not be searched with a bare substring match because `5` can match `15` or `50`; wrap multi-value strings with delimiters and search for the delimited token. Keep the server-side PageParameter filter path working too so first load, no-JavaScript, and crawlers agree with the client-side state.
title: Normalize GUID casing and delimit short IDs in client-side Rock filters

distilled_summary: Before adding more ConnectionRequest statuses or rebuilding Rock's native connection board list, check whether the needed visibility can be represented with activity badges, person attributes, connection attributes, requirements, or list-view fields. Extra statuses can make the board harder to operate when the value is only a checklist or visibility signal. Preserve native Rock board behavior where possible, and reserve new statuses for true lifecycle states that change ownership, timing, or operational next steps.
title: Use connection-card signals before adding more board statuses

distilled_summary: Connection status automation pairs a source status, destination status, and DataView; the job updates the current requests returned by that DataView. Keep the DataView deterministic and idempotent: include the current source status in the filter, avoid fixed one-time cutoff dates unless intentionally backfilling, and return only records that should still move if the job is retried. After bulk migrations or manual changes, validate destination status counts, connection state consistency, and ServiceJob history so a stale DataView does not keep moving the wrong requests.
title: Keep ConnectionStatusAutomation DataViews deterministic and validate job results

distilled_summary: The Lava `CreateShortLink` filter can create persistent short links, so treat its arguments as operational configuration rather than harmless display formatting. Before using it in communications or public pages, verify the current Rock syntax, the target site, overwrite behavior, random length, category, and pinning options in a non-production or controlled case. A shifted optional argument can silently create links with the wrong site or option values, so inspect the generated short-link row and final URL before bulk sending.
title: Preflight CreateShortLink argument order before using generated links operationally

distilled_summary: For seasonal workflow forms that present a reusable list of topics, quarters, roles, or group categories, a DefinedValue attribute can act as the visibility switch instead of creating a new DefinedType every season. Store stable options in the DefinedType, add a boolean or scoped attribute such as display-in-this-season, and have the form data source filter by that attribute. The operating runbook should include updating the option attributes and verifying the rendered dropdown so retired options do not remain selectable and new options do not require code changes.
title: Use DefinedValue attributes to gate seasonal workflow options

distilled_summary: A workflow selector can store values that came from one DefinedType even when the canonical attribute or report logic expects another DefinedType. That mismatch may not block form submission, but it can confuse reports, maintenance scripts, and future data-source changes. Before hardening a workflow or report, compare the field type configuration, selector SQL or Lava source, stored AttributeValue format, and downstream joins to DefinedValue so the selected value and reported value come from the same intentional source.
title: DefinedValue source mismatches can work at runtime but confuse reporting

distilled_summary: For forgot-username or password-reset communications, build Lava around the results collection and the user accounts actually returned for each person instead of assuming a single person-level reset flag is enough. Filter to local database-login accounts when the email should exclude passwordless or external-provider accounts, and remove debug output before production because reset-related merge data can expose operationally sensitive details. Always test with accounts that cover local login, passwordless, and external-provider cases.
title: Filter password-reset communication output by the returned user accounts

distilled_summary: For group-tree metrics, the reporting category may belong to a parent or coach group rather than each reporting group. Build the metric query or report so each qualifying group resolves the nearest ancestor with the configured reporting-category attribute, then aggregate by that inherited category. This keeps category maintenance at the operational level where leaders actually manage the tree, while avoiding uncategorized child groups or double-counted rollups when the group hierarchy changes.
title: Derive group metric reporting categories from the nearest configured ancestor

distilled_summary: For authenticated Helix active-search pages, keep the list endpoint responsible for the shell, filters, loading indicator, and first render, then keep the active-search endpoint responsible for reading PageParameter filters, running the bounded query, and returning only the inner rows or cards. Do not re-render the form, nav, or outer target container from the partial endpoint. Use `hx-include`, a single target container, a loading indicator, and explicit pagination state so filter changes and next/previous controls behave deterministically.
title: Keep Helix active-search endpoints focused on inner result HTML

distilled_summary: In Helix Lava endpoint work, verify the rendering context before using Lava's javascript or stylesheet commands. A tag that works in a page-rendered block may not emit usable assets from an endpoint response, especially when the endpoint is rendered through HTMX or another partial-response pattern. Prefer loading shared libraries once in the host shell, defining CSS variables or shared styles there, and keeping endpoint output resilient with inline fallback styles or guards such as checking for a charting library before initializing. Test both direct endpoint execution and the hosted page path.
title: Do not assume Lava javascript and stylesheet tags work inside Helix endpoints

distilled_summary: For Helix tables with HTMX filters, column sorting, and optional auto-refresh, keep sort state in the server-rendered results partial instead of a custom browser-only variable. Have the partial emit hidden sort and direction inputs, have filter requests include those inputs, and have each sortable header call the results endpoint with its next sort and direction query values. This keeps sorting, filtering, and refresh requests using the same server-side contract. For nullable columns such as room, group, assignment, or last activity, add an explicit null or blank bucket in the server-side ORDER BY so first-click ascending sorts show assigned/actionable values first and blanks at the bottom.
title: Let Helix results partials own table sort state

distilled_summary: On Rock pages where inline script tags are stripped or unreliable, prefer HTMX's declarative `hx-on:*` event attributes for small UI behaviors such as opening a modal after a swap, responding to HTMX lifecycle events, or handling a custom event from a swapped fragment. Verify the target route's sanitizer behavior, the HTMX event name, and the rendered markup as an anonymous visitor and as the intended role. Keep security decisions server-side; `hx-on` is a presentation pattern, not an authorization layer.
title: Use declarative hx-on behavior on sanitized Helix or CMS routes

distilled_summary: When a group metric answers historical questions, do not aggregate only the current Group and GroupMember rows. Evaluate each metric date against Rock's date dimension and the historical group/member snapshots, then aggregate records that were active and qualifying at that point in time. If the metric also depends on inherited group metadata, resolve that classification per group before the final aggregation so each group's partition is stable for the metric date. Verify the output by comparing current-period totals against a live group count and older-period totals against known historical changes.
title: Use point-in-time group tables for historical group metrics

distilled_summary: When a Rock CMS or Helix page renders a list or shell first and loads detail content later through HTMX, do not assume crawlers will see metadata emitted by the swapped fragment. Put canonical URLs, Open Graph tags, JSON-LD, title metadata, and other crawl-critical output on the route that serves the initial page response, or provide a server-rendered detail route that contains the metadata before any HTMX enhancement runs. Verify the anonymous first response and the rendered browser state separately.
title: Put SEO metadata on the host page when detail content is loaded by HTMX

distilled_summary: If a Rock CMS or Helix page stores UI state such as list/grid view, toggles, or expansion state in `sessionStorage` or `localStorage`, remember that an HTMX swap replaces the rendered controls. Re-apply state after `htmx:afterSwap`, or encode the state in URL parameters so the server can render the correct classes and ARIA state. Test the first render, swapped render, refresh, and back-button behavior; otherwise the data can be correct while the visible controls show stale state.
title: Re-sync local UI state after HTMX swaps replace rendered controls

distilled_summary: When troubleshooting a Helix Lava Application, include the application-level configuration rigging field in the preflight. Treat empty configuration as an explicit empty JSON object (`{}`), not as an unknown or null value, and verify the stored rigging is valid JSON before assuming an endpoint or content block problem. Configuration rigging is intended for stable application settings that are made available to backend endpoints and frontend content blocks; it is not a place for secrets or frequently changing data. If a Helix app fails while resolving configuration, inspect the LavaApplication record, the rigging JSON, and whether the values are environment-specific before changing endpoint code.
title: Validate LavaApplication configuration rigging as non-null JSON

distilled_summary: For Helix Lava Endpoints that inherit or use application-level security, troubleshoot authorization at the parent LavaApplication as well as the page, block, and endpoint. A page can be visible and a content block can be present while the endpoint still fails for anonymous or non-admin users if the parent application lacks the intended execute/view authorization. Before calling an endpoint public-ready, inspect the endpoint SecurityMode, the parent LavaApplication authorization rows, and test with an anonymous browser plus the intended authenticated role. Do not treat admin override success as proof that public or staff access is configured correctly.
title: Check parent LavaApplication authorization for ApplicationView endpoints

distilled_summary: When a workflow template combines nested conditions, assignments, and alternate branches on adjacent lines, a parser failure or silent branch bug can appear far from the branch that caused it. For production workflow forms and emails, split complicated `{% if %}`, `{% assign %}`, and alternate-branch logic into small, explicit blocks that can be previewed independently. This makes Rock's Lava parser errors easier to localize and reduces the chance that one conditional assignment changes the behavior of a later branch.
title: Favor simple Lava condition blocks when workflow templates parse unpredictably

distilled_summary: Helix Lava Endpoints use an enabled-command allow-list. If an endpoint template calls commands such as `workflowactivate`, SQL, Rock Entity, entity modify, HTTP response, or render-endpoint helpers, first verify that the endpoint's EnabledLavaCommands value includes exactly the commands the template needs. A command that works in one Lava surface or block does not prove it is enabled inside a specific Lava Endpoint. Keep command lists narrow, use read-only methods for read endpoints, enable CSRF on state-changing endpoints, and retest under the intended runtime security context after changing the allow-list.
title: Verify LavaEndpoint enabled commands before debugging endpoint logic

distilled_summary: A Lava parser error can be reported at the line where parsing finally fails, not necessarily where the malformed tag began. If a workflow email or endpoint reports an unexpected end-of-tag error on a harmless-looking line, inspect previous filters and attribute expressions for an unclosed quote, missing delimiter, or incomplete filter argument. This is especially common in communication templates where a broken `Replace` or formatting filter can make the raw Lava error appear in the outbound message.
title: Inspect earlier Lava filters when a parser error points at a later line

distilled_summary: For Rock metrics with SQL as the source, document the exact output contract and operating window instead of treating the query as a one-off report. The query should return the metric value, metric date/time grain, and every configured partition column in the order expected by the metric. Use an intentional first-run backfill window, then shorten the scheduled query to an incremental window. Keep validation totals by partition and date grain so future changes can prove that MetricValue rows were loaded at the expected cadence without duplicate or missing periods.
title: Treat SQL-backed metrics as a contract plus an operating process

distilled_summary: Rock Mobile content can be rendered from bundled shell content or processed dynamically, and the available Lava context changes with those block settings. Before using `CurrentPerson`, secure lookups, page parameters, or database-backed personalization in a mobile Content block, verify Dynamic Content, Process Lava on Server, enabled Lava commands, and the intended context entity. If content is bundled into the shell download, do not assume the same authenticated server-side context or freshness that a dynamic server-rendered block would have.
title: Check Rock Mobile Content block processing context before relying on CurrentPerson

distilled_summary: When Lava outputs XAML for Rock Mobile, escape any text that can contain content titles, user-entered strings, URLs, ampersands, quotes, apostrophes, or other markup-sensitive characters. Use the appropriate Lava escaping and URL encoding filters before putting values into XAML attributes or command/page parameters. Test with titles and names that contain punctuation so a single record cannot break the rendered mobile page or command parameter payload.
title: Escape user, title, and URL text before inserting it into Rock Mobile XAML

distilled_summary: When a Rock modify-entity Lava command creates an invalid entity, the failed object can remain tracked in the same render context and cause later unrelated saves to fail with the original validation error. A dbtransaction can roll back the database work inside its block, but it should not be treated as a reset for a previously poisoned render context. Put risky creates late, isolate experiments in a separate render, check ModifyResult.Success after every command, and bail out immediately on failure. For multi-entity deploy scripts, prefer an idempotent pattern: look up the entity, create only if missing, re-query the canonical ID, then write children.
title: A failed modify command can poison later writes in the same Lava render

distilled_summary: If modifyperson appears to do nothing from a Lava endpoint, first verify that the command is executing against the intended Person record. In flows that start from alias GUIDs, anonymous submissions, or workflow-created people, resolve the current PersonId before writing and read back the saved values before blaming the command. For conditional forms, also pre-load existing person attribute values and use them as fallbacks when a path omits fields; otherwise a later submission can overwrite prior path-specific attributes with blanks. This is especially important when a workflow and an endpoint both participate in identity resolution or person updates.
title: Resolve the person and preserve omitted attributes before using modifyperson

distilled_summary: When chaining Rock modify-entity Lava commands in an endpoint, use the default ModifyResult object and capture ModifyResult.Object.Id or Guid immediately after each command. Some entity commands expose typed result accessors, but the typed name is not a portable contract across every entity. Likewise, endpoint rendering can behave differently from Lava Tester when using custom return variable names. For dependent writes, check ModifyResult.Success, store the canonical parent ID right away, and stop the render if a required parent write fails instead of carrying a blank, zero, or unverified result into child rows.
title: Capture ModifyResult.Object immediately for portable Lava endpoint writes

distilled_summary: For a Rock-backed public AI or Helix concierge, keep the approved route or handoff registry broader than the fuzzy search-memory corpus. Route registries may need safe public handoffs for login, forms, giving, registration, group join, or other action paths, but those rows should not automatically become semantic-search material. Build a smaller upload or retrieval package that includes only public answerable content, approved public pages, public content metadata, and source-reviewed summaries; exclude account, auth, form, payment, registration, check-in, external account-invite, GUID-bearing, private-media, raw transcript, and staff-only patterns. The AI layer should retrieve bounded snippets through a server-side adapter and trusted renderer, while exact actions still route through the approved Rock page, form, or workflow boundary.
title: Separate public AI search memory from route and handoff registries

distilled_summary: When building a public Rock-backed concierge or Helix UI, avoid treating a full Rock page iframe as the long-term integration contract. Full-page iframe embedding can be blocked by Content Security Policy frame-ancestors rules, and sandboxed iframes can also change origin behavior in ways that break HTMX or authenticated page assumptions. Prefer a page-hosted Lava Application Content block, a purpose-built Helix endpoint, or a small read-only adapter that returns only approved public fields to the trusted renderer. If an existing Rock application must remain available, route users to it as a top-level page and keep any person-backed form state, POST endpoints, SMS verification, workflow activation, and mutation paths behind a separate explicit test or launch protocol.
title: Avoid embedding full Rock pages as public concierge app surfaces

distilled_summary: When migrating Rock Mobile XAML from Xamarin Forms to .NET MAUI, treat layout risks as separate recipes. Removing AndExpand is not the same as preserving expansion behavior; layouts that genuinely need expansion usually need Grid rows or columns. ScrollView inside an unconstrained StackLayout may stop scrolling and should be bounded by Grid. MAUI also changes implicit grid rows, default spacing, CSS property prefixes, and hard size requests. Inventory each pattern, classify which changes are safe for older shells, version-gate MAUI-only controls, and visually verify pages with real shell rendering rather than trusting a text replacement.
title: Separate MAUI layout fixes instead of doing one blanket XAML conversion

distilled_summary: For Rock Mobile migrations that need to serve Xamarin and .NET MAUI markup at the same time, put the Lava version gate inside the page or block XAML fragment that the shell will download. Do not rely on a global page-routing gate unless you have verified it executes before the shell parses that fragment. Also verify the actual Device.ShellVersion format in the target shell; do not assume the value will match a marketing version number. The safe pattern is to parse the observed version string, render only the branch compatible with that shell, and test both old and new shells from the same Rock content source.
title: Put Rock Mobile shell version gates inside the XAML that is rendered

distilled_summary: Before changing a Rock configuration or entity, decide which update surface is the real owner of the behavior. Use normal Rock API or REST-style updates for stable entity/controller changes, Lava entity commands for admin-run deploys or workflow/action configuration changes, Obsidian BlockActions when the block action is the actual UI save path, and file-content deployment only for endpoint, block, or server-file content. Treat read-only SQL as verification evidence, not the mutation path. This preflight reduces partial writes and avoids bypassing validation or related side effects that Rock expects on the intended surface.
title: Choose the Rock update surface before changing production data

distilled_summary: Seasonal operations often use a leader-facing workflow plus a review or follow-up workflow. When rolling to a new quarter, campaign, or season, update defaults and labels in every linked WorkflowType, not only the form users submit first. Check visible copy, hidden default attributes, review workflow defaults, and any action criteria that use the seasonal value. Then verify that no prior-season workflow instances remain open before the launch. Otherwise new submissions can carry the new label while review queues or reports still write the previous season.
title: Update seasonal workflow defaults across every linked workflow type

distilled_summary: A workflow form that supports both self-applicants and family-member applicants should not assume that every applicant context has the same contact fields available. For child or family-member flows, email and mobile values may belong to a parent or may not be present on the selected person. Required flags, validation, and downstream communication actions should branch on the applicant mode, then separately validate whether the chosen communication target has the fields needed for that path. This avoids blocking valid family submissions or writing placeholder contact data just to satisfy a self-applicant form shape.
title: Make workflow form required fields match the applicant context

distilled_summary: For volunteer onboarding, shadowing often needs to affect printed badges, check-in visibility, team rosters, or ministry-specific overrides. A status label alone may not be enough. Consider temporary per-ministry shadowing groups for the shadowing phase, then manually or automatically promote people to placement groups once each team's requirements are complete. Verify how group membership, badge logic, check-in labels, and connection status interact before relying on status text as the only operational signal.
title: Use temporary groups for shadowing state when badges or check-in visibility matter

distilled_summary: If a Rock attribute, block setting, confirmation field, or CMS value stores Lava or Lava shortcodes as text, outputting the value directly may display the shortcode markup instead of executing it. When the design intentionally allows that stored content to execute, render it through an explicit Lava-processing step such as the `RunLava` filter and verify the page, block, or endpoint security context first. Because running stored Lava can execute commands or expose data depending on the surface and enabled commands, review who can edit the stored value, what commands are available, and whether the output is public before enabling this pattern.
title: Render stored Lava intentionally when shortcodes appear as raw text

distilled_summary: SystemCommunication sender fields can render Lava, but they still behave like constrained message header fields. Keep `From`, `FromName`, and related sender values short, valid for the target channel, and backed by a static fallback when complex alignment logic would exceed field limits or produce an invalid email address. Verify the saved communication template, the rendered outbound message, and the channel-specific sender behavior before assigning the communication to a workflow, group scheduling confirmation, or other automated send.
title: Keep SystemCommunication sender fields compact and valid even when they contain Lava

distilled_summary: When a workflow form changes selector values, defaults, or hidden fields, review any downstream action criteria that still reference the previous payload vocabulary. A condition that checks for an old enum value will not fire if the current form now sends an empty string, a GUID, a DefinedValue id, or a different label. Before troubleshooting a skipped email, activation, or update action, inspect the actual submitted AttributeValue values and compare them to each action's criteria rather than relying on the form label users see.
title: Keep workflow action criteria aligned to the current form payload values

distilled_summary: Workflow attributes should be scoped to the intended WorkflowType through the correct entity type and qualifier. If an attribute with the same key exists without the expected qualifier, defaults or page-parameter writes can create misleading AttributeValue rows that appear in one UI surface but are invisible to SQL that reads the scoped workflow attribute. Before adding defaults, copying values, or repairing a workflow, check `EntityTypeId`, `EntityTypeQualifierColumn`, and `EntityTypeQualifierValue`; migrate only values that can be tied to the intended workflow type, and avoid bulk-moving default-value noise from unrelated workflows.
title: Verify workflow attribute scope before adding defaults or repairing values

distilled_summary: In rerunnable workflow deploy scripts, treat `WorkflowActionType.WorkflowFormId` as the source of truth after the action type is saved. Do not attach `WorkflowActionFormAttribute` rows from an unverified create result or an assumed form ID. Re-query the action type, confirm its form exists, then attach child form attributes to that saved form ID. This prevents child fields from being wired to a blank, stale, or transient object when a deploy is re-run or partially repaired.
title: Re-query the saved workflow form ID before attaching form fields

distilled_summary: If a Workflow Form action captures user-entered workflow attributes and the next action immediately uses SQL to read those values from `AttributeValue`, add a Persist Workflow step between them and test the saved rows. The workflow UI or in-memory Lava state can show the new value before the database row is available to a SQL action. If SQL still cannot see the value, verify the attribute's entity type and qualifier, not just the visible attribute name.
title: Persist a workflow before SQL reads attributes submitted by the previous form action

distilled_summary: When a workflow action renders Lava-driven HTML to PDF, local browser or local `wkhtmltopdf` output may not match the production Rock renderer, plugin wrapper, operating system, or renderer version. Use local rendering for fast iteration, but make the Rock-generated PDF the acceptance artifact. For layout-sensitive certificates or forms, prefer a small number of dynamic text overlays on a fixed coordinate system, and verify the final PDF visually from the workflow action before launching the template.
title: Treat Rock workflow PDF output as the source of truth for PDF template layout

distilled_summary: When reading a workflow attribute in Lava with the `Object` option, verify the attribute's field type and returned object shape before assuming it is a PersonAlias wrapper. For Person field-type attributes, the object may already be a Person object, so code such as `.Person.NickName` can fail or render blank where `.NickName` is the correct path. For workflow emails, endpoint detail views, and status screens, test the Lava against a real workflow instance and confirm whether the stored value is a person alias GUID, person GUID, or another field-specific value before building property chains.
title: Inspect workflow Person attribute object shape before chaining PersonAlias properties

distilled_summary: When a workflow form uses visible helper selectors and separate canonical storage attributes, validate all three layers before editing: the form fields and required flags, the Set Attribute or equivalent actions that copy selector values into canonical attributes, and the DefinedValue, SQL, Lava, or campus data sources that feed the selectors. A workflow can appear functional while reports or downstream actions read a different canonical attribute than the one users selected.
title: Validate workflow selector fields, canonical attributes, and data sources together

distilled_summary: A Single-Select workflow attribute can display a readable label while storing an internal value that later actions need, such as a DefinedValue ID, saved account ID, or other lookup key. When copying that stored value to another workflow attribute or using it in a validation query, use the raw attribute value rather than the formatted display output. Test with a label that differs from the stored ID and verify the downstream attribute contains the expected internal value before running dependent actions.
title: Use RawValue when copying a Single-Select workflow attribute that stores an internal ID

distilled_summary: When using the Lava `workflowactivate` command, treat extra key/value parameters as a contract with the target workflow or activity attributes. If a submitted parameter does not match an attribute key on the workflow/activity being activated, do not assume Rock will warn loudly or preserve that value. Before relying on the activated workflow, compare the rendered `workflowactivate` parameter names to the workflow/activity attribute keys, remove dead parameters, add any missing attributes intentionally, and verify the created workflow's AttributeValue rows or rendered workflow state after launch. This is especially important for form submit endpoints that collect many fields and pass them into a helper workflow.
title: Treat workflowactivate parameters as an attribute-key contract

distilled_summary: A scheduled workflow-launch job can report failures even when earlier actions in the launched workflow already changed data, such as adding a person to a group, sending a communication, or writing an attribute. When diagnosing a failed count, inspect the workflow action order, the action log, and the expected side effects before retrying. Gate late cleanup or notification actions with clear criteria, and make duplicate-suppression queries account for side effects that may have succeeded before the final error.
title: Check for successful side effects before treating a WorkflowLauncher failure as a full rollback
